6. Key Insights & Recommendations

Top Findings

1. Workout Participation Holds at ~100%: Roughly 100.0% of daily records include a workout. Gender differences are modest (Male: 100.0%, Female: 100.0%). Product implication: the ~0% of non-workout days represents a large activation surface — targeted nudges on rest days could lift participation without cannibalizing existing habits.
2. Steps Track Strongly with Calories (r = 0.97): Daily steps remain the single best predictor of calorie burn. Users averaging 10,574 steps/day burn 617 kcal. Product implication: step-count goals remain the most intuitive engagement lever; consider dynamic daily targets that adapt to recent trends.
3. Mood Distribution Skews Toward "Tired" (33.2%): "Tired" is the a prevalent mood. Tired users still participate in workouts at 100.0%. Product implication: recovery-focused features (gentle workout suggestions, sleep improvement tips) could address a large segment that is active but fatigued.
4. Sleep is Relatively Stable Across Groups: Average sleep of 6.99 hours varies little by mood or stress level, suggesting that self-reported wellness perception diverges from measured sleep quantity. Product implication: sleep quality metrics (not just duration) would add value — consider integrating sleep stage data if available from trackers.
5. Stress is Weakly Related to Activity Volume: Average stress (5.45) does not drop dramatically with higher step counts. Product implication: "more exercise = less stress" messaging may overstate the relationship in this cohort. Mindfulness or breathing features may be a better stress-reduction pathway.
